notes: Parole Board JR on burden of proof and Article 5; facts and outcome are clear though Article 5 compatibility was addressed only obiter.

enrichment.short_title: Parole Board release refusal: burden of proof and Article 5
key_facts: Sean Henry was convicted of murder aged 17 and sentenced to detention at Her Majesty's Pleasure with a nine-year tariff.
After release on licence in 1999 he was recalled and later found in possession of heroin while in open conditions.
The Discretionary Lifer Panel refused release in August 2003, finding the risk to life and limb remained too high.
The sole ground of judicial review was that the Panel wrongly placed the burden on the claimant to prove he was safe to release rather than on the Secretary of State.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a Parole Board decision refusing to direct release of a discretionary life prisoner.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the case was not borderline and the Panel's reference to onus reflected the claimant's conduct rather than a general misdirection on burden of proof.
enrichment.ratio: Where a Parole Board decision letter is read as a whole, a statement that the prisoner must demonstrate he is safe to release may reflect the particular facts rather than an erroneous reversal of the section 28(6)(b) test; in a non-borderline case the Article 5 compatibility of placing the onus on the prisoner does not arise for decision.
legal_issues: Whether the Parole Board erred by placing the burden of proof on the prisoner
Whether section 28(6)(b) of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997 is incompatible with Article 5 ECHR
Whether risk assessment in parole decisions involves a burden of proof at all
Whether Comerford and Reid are distinguishable in relation to detention at Her Majesty's Pleasure

notes: Article 6 delay remedy after Attorney General's Reference (No 2 of 2001); DPP conceded breach and reduction in disqualification is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 delay remedy in postal guilty plea speeding case
key_facts: Miller pleaded guilty by post to three speeding offences in February 1999 but was not sentenced until September 2001 after a two-year delay in executing an unlawfully issued warrant.
The justices rejected his Article 6 abuse of process arguments and disqualified him for 12 months under the totting-up provisions.
On case stated, the DPP conceded there had been unreasonable delay in breach of Article 6(1) including delay over stating the case.
Following Attorney General's Reference (No 2 of 2001), quashing the convictions was no longer available and the appropriate remedy was reduction in sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' court decisions on Article 6 delay and wasted costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; one-year disqualification reduced to five months as a just and appropriate Article 6 remedy, and the DPP ordered to pay £375 plus VAT for wasted costs below; half of appeal costs from central funds assessed at £3,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where Article 6 has been breached by unreasonable delay but a fair hearing remained possible and it was not unfair to try the defendant, convictions should not be quashed; a reduction in disqualification under section 35(1) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 may be a just and proportionate remedy, taking exceptional hardship from delay into account.
legal_issues: Whether delay rendered the prosecution an abuse of process or breach of Article 6
What remedy is appropriate where Article 6 is breached after conviction
Whether the appellant should have been permitted to change his plea to not guilty
Whether the justices should have awarded costs of the wasted costs application
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference (No 2 of 2001) [2003] UKHL 68
R v Lord Advocate [2003] 2 WLR 317
Fay v Fay [1982] 2 All ER 922

notes: Short supplemental judgment on post-appeal relief; pragmatic fresh tribunal order and costs split are clear.

enrichment.short_title: GMC appeal: pragmatic remittal to fresh tribunal
key_facts: Mahfouz appealed against a GMC Professional Conduct Committee's refusal to discharge itself after reading prejudicial newspaper articles and its refusal to adjourn.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the discharge challenge but allowed the appeal on the refusal to grant a short adjournment.
After judgment, counsel sought relief requiring the proceedings to be heard by a totally fresh tribunal.
The court ordered pragmatic remittal to a fresh tribunal for cost-saving reasons, not because the appellant was entitled to that relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further submissions on relief following a Court of Appeal judgment in a GMC professional conduct judicial review appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Matter remitted to a fresh tribunal as a pragmatic solution; appellant ordered to pay 50% of respondents' costs; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused; interim costs payment of £10,000 ordered pending detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where an appeal on adjournment has succeeded but the appellant was not entitled to a fresh tribunal as of right, the court may nevertheless remit to a fresh tribunal for pragmatic reasons to avoid further expense and difficulty, without treating that order as a victory for the appellant or criticism of the original tribunal.
legal_issues: What relief follows from a successful appeal on refusal to adjourn GMC proceedings
Whether fairness required a fresh tribunal after evidence was given in the appellant's absence
Whether alleged bias in the transcript justified a new panel
Appropriate costs order where the appeal succeeded only in part

notes: Child support liability order limitation point; statutory construction and Regentford analogy are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Child support liability order six-year limitation period
key_facts: Phillip Sutherland was assessed in October 1997 to pay child maintenance backdated to May 1995.
By 2002 arrears exceeded £18,000 and the Child Support Agency applied for a liability order in September 2002.
The appellant argued Regulation 28(2) barred proceedings because the first sums became due more than six years before the complaint was laid.
The magistrates made the liability order and the Secretary of State was awarded costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated against a magistrates' court liability order for unpaid child support maintenance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; payments did not become due for limitation purposes until the maintenance assessment was notified in October 1997, and the magistrates were correct to make the liability order.
enrichment.ratio: Under Regulation 28(2) of the Child Support (Collection and Enforcement) Regulations 1992, the six-year period for instituting liability order proceedings runs from when payment became due in the sense of enforceable liability, which does not arise until a maintenance assessment is made rather than from the earlier general obligation under section 1(2) of the Child Support Act 1991.
legal_issues: When payment of child support maintenance becomes due for Regulation 28(2) limitation purposes
Whether payable and due bear different meanings in Regulations 27 and 28
Whether the magistrates could amend the amount claimed if part was out of time
Whether human rights were breached by making the liability order
linked_authorities: Regentford v Thanet District Council [2004] EWHC 246 (Admin)
Westminster City Council v O'Reilly

notes: Unsafe system of work finding upheld despite late unpleaded case; Part 36 costs discretion on unpleaded success point is well explained.

enrichment.short_title: Container ship ladder accident: unsafe system of work
key_facts: Electrical officer Wilson fell about eight feet from a walkway ladder on the container ship Tobias Maersk while taking reefer temperature readings.
The trial judge rejected the pleaded case on the Bay 28 ladder configuration but accepted a late argument that an unsafe system of work across seven other ladders had induced a dangerous habit.
Contributory negligence was assessed at 60%.
Maersk appealed on evidential support; Wilson cross-appealed on the judge's limited Part 36 costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a High Court judgment on liability and costs after a personal injury trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal on costs dismissed; there was sufficient evidence for the unsafe system finding and the judge was entitled to limit Part 36 costs because the successful point was raised very late.
enrichment.ratio: An employer may be liable where an unsafe system of work on most walkway ladders makes it reasonably foreseeable that an experienced seaman will habitually descend even a safer ladder unsafely; where a claimant succeeds on an unpleaded point raised only in closing submissions, the trial judge may justly exercise discretion under CPR Part 36.21 not to award full indemnity costs.
legal_issues: Whether the judge had evidence to find an unsafe system of work on unpleaded grounds
Whether identical ladder configurations across bays were established
Whether procedural unfairness invalidated the unsafe system finding
Whether CPR Part 36.21 required all prescribed costs orders once a Part 36 offer was beaten

notes: Novel non-party medical disclosure application; causation analysis is rich but the published judgment text appears truncated before final orders.

enrichment.short_title: Refusal to order non-party sibling medical disclosure in PI claim
key_facts: Claimant A suffered serious head and brain injuries as a passenger in a road accident and pursued a high-value loss-of-earnings claim.
His psychiatric condition was disputed, with experts considering genetic vulnerability because his brother B may have a similar disorder.
Defendant X applied under CPR 31.17 for disclosure of B's medical records to investigate causation of A's bipolar mood disorder.
Morland J held disclosure was likely to support X's case but was not necessary for fair disposal and he would in any event have refused to exercise discretion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under CPR 31.17 for disclosure of medical records of a non-party in a personal injury action.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; disclosure of a non-party's confidential medical data would require exceptional facts and safeguards could not overcome Article 8 and privacy concerns here.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a non-party's medical records are likely to support one party's case under CPR 31.17(3)(a), an order requires disclosure to be necessary for fair disposal or to save costs under CPR 31.17(3)(b); interference with a non-party's Article 8 rights and confidential medical data will only exceptionally be justified, especially where delay and alternative causation evidence weigh against disclosure.
legal_issues: Meaning of likely under CPR 31.17(3)(a) following Three Rivers DC v Bank of England (No 4)
Whether disclosure of a sibling's medical records was necessary for fair disposal
Whether Article 8 and Data Protection Act constraints were outweighed by safeguards
Effect of delay and existing expert evidence on exercise of discretion

notes: Large excise duty fraud and winding-up appeal; DSMEG validity, causation, and disputed-debt test are comprehensively analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Excise duty fraud assessments and Arena winding-up appeal

statutes_considered.title: Excise Duty Points (Duty Suspended Movement of Excise Goods) Regulations 2001

key_facts: Arena Corporation moved bonded alcoholic goods from English warehouses to purported destinations in Belgium and Italy using false accompanying administrative documents.
Customs assessed Arena for over £1.8 million excise duty under DSMEG Regulation 7(2) as jointly liable with the warehouse guarantor.
Customs petitioned to wind up Arena and Lawrence Collins J made a winding-up order and granted summary judgment against its controller Mr Schroeder.
Arena appealed contending Regulation 7(2) was invalid, no excise duty point occurred, and it had not caused any irregularity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a winding-up order and related summary judgment based on excise duty assessments pending before the VAT and Duties Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; Regulation 7(2) was valid, excise duty points arose, and there was no bona fide dispute on substantial grounds that Arena caused the irregularities.
enrichment.ratio: DSMEG Regulation 7(2) is consistent with Directive 92/12/EEC and intra vires section 1(4) of the Finance (No.2) Act 1992; a person who causes the underlying irregularity in a duty-suspended movement has sufficient connection with the goods to be jointly liable, but ownership and instruction to dispatch alone are insufficient without culpable causation of the diversion.
legal_issues: Validity of DSMEG Regulation 7(2) under EU law and the enabling statute
Whether an excise duty point arose under Regulations 3 or 4
What causation is required under Regulation 7(2)
Whether the Companies Court should determine a genuinely disputed excise duty debt

notes: Gypsy status planning appeal applying Wrexham; inspector's reasons held adequate without perversity challenge.

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy caravan site planning permission: status review
key_facts: Romany gypsies Rachel and Elizabeth Cooper obtained planning permission for gypsy caravan sites at Foxgrove and Blossom in Essex.
Basildon District Council challenged the Secretary of State's decision, arguing the inspector failed properly to apply Wrexham on nomadic habit of life.
The inspector found both women came from gypsy families, had travelled before settling, and retained gypsy status despite health and education restrictions.
Sir Richard Tucker dismissed the section 288 challenge and the Council appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a High Court decision dismissing a planning challenge to gypsy caravan site permissions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the inspector adequately considered whether the Coopers had abandoned their nomadic habit of life and his reasons were sufficient.
enrichment.ratio: Following Wrexham County Borough Council v The National Assembly for Wales, gypsy status is a functional question of whether applicants retain a nomadic habit of life at the date of the planning decision; temporary restrictions from illness or children's education do not necessarily mean abandonment if the inspector properly rejects a settled-life-with-no-prospect-of-resuming case.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector applied Wrexham correctly
Whether the inspector gave adequate reasons on future intention to resume travelling
Whether cross-examination evidence on abandonment was ignored
Whether gypsy status had been abandoned through local employment and settlement

linked_authorities: Wrexham County Borough Council v The National Assembly for Wales [2003] EWCA Civ 835

notes: Highway obstruction prosecution after DPP v Jones; magistrates' reasonableness finding upheld on wide Article 8-free facts.

enrichment.short_title: Highway burger trailer trading as reasonable use after Jones
key_facts: Osman Keskin operated the Cosmos burger and kebab trailer on Bramston Way nightly for about two and a half years, selling food from the highway.
Private prosecutor Scott laid informations alleging wilful obstruction of the highway on six dates in 2001 and 2002.
The justices found wilful obstruction but held Keskin had a reasonable excuse because traffic was minimal on the industrial estate and the road remained passable.
Scott appealed by case stated asking whether such use could be reasonable under section 137(1).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from acquittals on informations for wilful obstruction of the highway.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the magistrates were entitled to find the obstruction was reasonable in the circumstances after DPP v Jones.
enrichment.ratio: Following DPP v Jones, the public may use the highway for reasonable purposes not inconsistent with the primary right of passage; whether parking a food trailer for long nightly periods amounts to a reasonable excuse for obstruction under section 137(1) is a question of fact and degree for the magistrates, reviewable only if no reasonable bench could have reached that conclusion.
legal_issues: Whether long-term trailer trading can be a reasonable use of the highway after DPP v Jones
Whether the justices correctly applied the Hirst v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire approach
Whether the obstruction was de minimis or reasonably excused
Effect of police and local authority inaction on reasonableness

notes: Working Time holiday pay construction is detailed and authoritative; section 234 incorporation via regulation 16 is the central holding.

enrichment.short_title: Holiday pay excludes non-guaranteed compulsory overtime
key_facts: Mr Sturge's contract provided a basic 39-hour week but required substantial compulsory non-guaranteed overtime, typically about 58 to 60 hours weekly.
His employer paid annual leave at basic-hours rates, producing about two thirds of his normal weekly earnings.
Regulation 16 of the Working Time Regulations calculates holiday pay by reference to a week's pay under sections 221 to 224 of the Employment Rights Act 1996.
Section 234 defines normal working hours as fixed contractual hours unless overtime is guaranteed on both sides.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision upholding an employment tribunal on calculation of paid annual leave under the Working Time Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; regulation 16 incorporates section 234, so compulsory but non-guaranteed overtime is excluded from normal working hours and holiday pay.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 16(2) of the Working Time Regulations incorporates sections 221 to 224 of the Employment Rights Act 1996 together with the definition of normal working hours in section 234; Article 7 of the Working Time Directive leaves payment conditions to member states and does not require holiday pay to include overtime that the employer is not contractually bound to provide.
legal_issues: Meaning of normal working hours in sections 221 to 224 and section 234
Whether regulation 16 incorporates section 234 for holiday pay purposes
Whether a Marleasing conforming construction is required by Article 7 of the Directive
Whether sections 221 to 224 are workable without section 234
